title: Fuel Loading Begins at RAPP-8, India's Fourth Homegrown 700 MWe Nuclear Reactor
excerpt: Initial fuel loading has begun at the Rawatbhata reactor after regulatory clearance, moving India's fourth indigenous 700 MWe PHWR into nuclear commissioning — with commercial operation expected this financial year.
body:
• NPCIL has begun initial fuel loading at RAPP-8, the fourth indigenously built 700 MWe pressurised heavy water reactor, at Rawatbhata in Rajasthan.
  • Fuel insertion began after clearance from the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, formally moving the unit from construction and system testing into nuclear commissioning.
  • The unit is the fourth of 16 planned 700 MWe PHWRs; first criticality, staged power ascension and regulatory-verified tests will follow before commercial operation.
  • NPCIL expects RAPP-8 to enter commercial operation in the current financial year, adding 630 MWe net capacity to its fleet of 24 operating reactors.

The Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd has begun initial fuel loading at RAPP-8, its fourth indigenously built 700 MWe pressurised heavy water reactor (PHWR) at Rawatbhata in Rajasthan, marking the unit's formal shift from construction and system testing into nuclear commissioning.

The start of fuel insertion followed permission from the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, granted after safety evaluations, major system-integrity audits and site-readiness reviews met regulatory conditions.

RAPP-8 is the fourth of a planned 16 indigenous 700 MWe PHWRs, a standardised fleet designed for repeat deployment to shorten build and commissioning cycles and add predictable, low-carbon baseload power to the grid.

Context & Background

The road to fuel loading has been long. Construction of RAPP-8 began in September 2011 alongside its twin, RAPP-7, which achieved first criticality in September 2024, connected to the grid in March 2025 and entered commercial operation in April 2025, reaching its full 700 MW output this February.

The first two 700 MWe PHWRs in the series, Kakrapar units 3 and 4 in Gujarat, entered commercial operation in 2023-24. RAPP-8's schedule slipped partly because of extensive design reviews and safety upgrades ordered after the Fukushima accident in Japan, the government told Parliament in a written reply last December. Hot functional testing at the unit began this February, according to NPCIL.

The Rawatbhata site in Rajasthan's Chittorgarh district is one of India's oldest nuclear complexes: six of its eight units are currently operational, with unit 1 shut down and headed for decommissioning.

Impact & Analysis

NPCIL currently operates 24 reactors with a combined capacity of about 8.78 GWe, and has 17 more units under implementation. Each new 700 MWe unit adds roughly 630 MWe of net capacity — firm, round-the-clock power that wind and solar cannot match without storage.

The standardised PHWR-700 design is the workhorse of India's indigenous nuclear programme. Because the units are near-copies, lessons from Kakrapar and RAPP-7 feed directly into RAPP-8 and the ten more 700 MWe units sanctioned at sites including Gorakhpur in Haryana, Kaiga in Karnataka, Chutka in Madhya Pradesh and Mahi Banswara in Rajasthan.

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora, India's nuclear buildout is the quiet engine behind the country's energy security — the baseload power that keeps industry running and household electricity affordable as demand grows, and a core pillar of the clean-energy transition India has committed to internationally.

What's Next

After fuel loading comes the first approach to criticality — the moment nuclear fission begins — followed by staged power ascension and regulatory-verified tests. NPCIL expects to seek commercial operation within the current financial year, a milestone that would put four of the 16 planned PHWR-700s into service.
